projects.title: lab-chat — a private chat server for AI agents
projects.summary: A self-hosted Matrix server where six coding agents notify me, ask for approval, and hand work to each other, where lab alerts land, and where I chat with a sandboxed Hermes agent. No agent holds a chat credential: they call an MCP bridge that runs one sandbox per trust domain, and the chat Hermes goes through a proxy that holds its token and allowlists the API. Nothing leaves the workstation.
highlights: Closed by construction — federation, registration, guests, URL previews and stats reporting are off, and Synapse plus its database sit on an internal Docker network with no route to the internet, the LAN or DNS; one nginx gateway publishes Element and the client API on loopback and answers 404 for federation and the admin API

Agents never hold a Matrix token — a 6-tool MCP bridge (notify, ask_human/get_answer, post, read, list_rooms) maps each client's own token, or for containers the private network it calls from, to exactly one chat account

One sandbox per trust domain — trusted host agents, the sandboxed local Claude Code, Hermes and Turnstone each get their own bridge process in an srt sandbox with no network and read access to only their own bot tokens; the code runs from hash-checked copies outside the repo the agents can write

Room rules enforced twice — one rooms.json drives both the bridge's ACL and Synapse's membership and power levels, so contained agents can neither read nor post in trusted rooms even with a valid token

Built for prompt injection — only messages the server authenticated as the human count as instructions; other agents' text comes back labelled [UNTRUSTED trust:account] with terminal escapes and bidi characters stripped, agent posts are notices (bots don't answer them, so no reply loops), and writes and pings to the human are rate-limited
Lab alerts in the same place — Prometheus fires into Alertmanager, which posts firing and resolved alerts to an #alerts room over an internal network with exactly two members

Chat with a sandboxed Hermes — a separate Hermes answers me in its own room through Hermes's Matrix gateway; a mitmproxy add-on holds its token and lets it only read and reply in that one room, it runs unprivileged with read-only config and tool policy and no internet, and risky commands wait for my ✅ in the chat

projects.html: The question was simple: how do agents reach me, and each other, without handing a third party a command channel into them? The answer was a chat server I own end to end, plus a bridge that keeps chat credentials out of every agent. The full design, the threat model and what went wrong along the way are in the write-up linked below.

projects.title: Nemo Console — one page for ten NVIDIA AI systems
projects.summary: A local console that monitors, configures and tests ten NVIDIA systems, from routing and serving to GPU telemetry, sandboxes, guardrails and evals. Config edits are validated, backed up and rolled back if the system comes up unhealthy.
highlights: Ten systems in v0.3.0, grouped as routing (NeMo Switchyard, NeMo Relay), engines and load (Dynamo, DCGM, AIPerf), safety and sandboxing (NeMo Guardrails, OpenShell) and evaluation and data (SkillEvaluator, NeMo Evaluator, Data Designer)

One adapter per system behind a system-agnostic core; the UI renders from descriptors (status, metrics, config files, parameters, actions, playground), so each new system was one adapter file plus a small view

Config edits validate, diff, back up, write atomically, restart the system and roll back on their own if it comes up unhealthy — Switchyard and Relay routes, the DCGM exporter's field list, NeMo Guardrails rails and the AIPerf and Evaluator presets

Security checks surface as problems with one exact fix: a DCGM exporter older than 4.8.3 (CVE-2026-47483) or an open /debug/pprof, an OpenShell sandbox network that is not internal, a Guardrails server that can reach the internet

Trust files stay read-only (OpenShell's sandbox policy, Relay's plugin policy); NeMo Guardrails rails are editable, but a change that removes a rail needs an explicit marker line that lands in the diff and the audit log
Disruptive actions need confirmation: GPU diagnostics in a hardened throwaway container, AIPerf load tests, Evaluator benchmark runs, gateway start/stop

Security middleware on every call: loopback bind, Host allowlist, same-origin checks, CSRF header, hashed bearer keys with admin and viewer roles, strict CSP, and one argv-only process runner with a bare-name binary allowlist
Every claim in the docs is labelled implemented, verified-live or unverified; an independent security review of the 0.3.0 additions found no high-severity issue and every finding was fixed
A browser end-to-end test (the real backend and a headless Chrome, every page and tab) runs in CI and in a pre-push hook that refuses code it has not passed

projects.html:
My lab runs NVIDIA's routing layer (NeMo Switchyard and NeMo Relay), Dynamo, a DCGM exporter on six machines, an OpenShell sandbox gateway, a NeMo Guardrails server and four NVIDIA command-line tools (SkillEvaluator, Data Designer, AIPerf, NeMo Evaluator). Each is configured differently — TOML, YAML, CSV, compose files, systemd units — and a bad edit to a routing file takes routing down for every agent at once. Nemo Console puts them on one page: see what each system is doing, change its config with a diff and an automatic rollback, run its checks, and send a test request through it.

What 0.3.1 fixed

After the 0.3.0 update, the five newest pages showed "Something went wrong" in a browser that had used an older version. The console served its files with no caching instructions, so the browser kept an old shared module and paired it with the new pages; one missing function was enough to stop all five from loading. Every file is now checked with the server on each load.

Unit tests could not have seen that, so 0.3.1 adds a browser test: it starts the real backend, signs in with a fresh key, and opens every page and tab in a headless Chrome, failing on any error screen, script error, server error or file served without that header. It runs in CI and in a pre-push hook that refuses to push code it has not passed. Its first run from a fresh clone, with no lab next to it, found two more bugs: a Dynamo parameter preview that crashed with a server error and Config tabs that reported "Something went wrong" for systems that are simply not deployed.

What 0.3.0 added

Six systems joined the original four: Data Designer, OpenShell, DCGM, AIPerf, NeMo Guardrails and NeMo Evaluator. The release also fixed three bugs found along the way: nemo-console stop hung while a browser held a live event stream, three status caches skipped their check for the first minute after a reboot (a fresh CI runner caught it), and per-GPU charts were empty because a label held spaces.

It was written against one deployment, and the README says so: container names and paths are settings or constants, and only the parts marked verified-live were exercised against the real systems.

The write-up linked below covers what this console was first built to watch: routing a coding agent between a fast model and a large one.

projects.title: Agent Hub — one place for what your coding agents know and may do
projects.summary: Shared instructions, skills, subagents, MCP servers, permissions and egress for Claude Code, opencode, Hermes Agent and Turnstone. Edit, commit, plan, apply — with a policy floor content can only make stricter.
highlights: A git repository of declarative files is the source of truth; the hub compiles it into each client's native format (.claude/skills, .opencode/agent, AGENTS.md, Hermes and Turnstone stages) instead of being a service the agents query
Edit, commit, plan, apply: a plan renders the committed tree per client and shows the diff; apply writes only from that plan, only after confirmation, and refuses if anything moved since
A policy floor outside the content repo — credential paths denied, egress deny-by-default, no unscanned MCP server, no catch-all shell allow — that content can only tighten

Import first: it reads what each client already has, and a file edited outside the hub becomes a conflict that is skipped, never silently overwritten; every overwritten file is backed up and rollback restores the last apply
Optional skill evaluation before import with NVIDIA SkillEvaluator, and an import gate that can require a clean static security scan
New clients without code: a declarative YAML spec validated live in the add-client wizard
projects.html:
Each coding agent keeps its instructions, skills, subagents, MCP servers and permissions in a different format and place. In my lab that is Claude Code, opencode, Hermes Agent and Turnstone, and shared content drifted between them with nothing showing what any one of them was allowed to do. Agent Hub treats that configuration like infrastructure code: reviewed in git, planned, applied with a diff, and checked against a floor of rules that content cannot loosen.

The README names the limit plainly: the hub cannot protect you from an unsandboxed client that runs as your own user. hubctl doctor reports what is exposed on the host.

projects.title: Jobpilot — AI job-search copilot
projects.summary: A local job-search copilot: postings are screened for prompt injection, scored by an explainable matcher, and turned into tailored resumes and cover letters that fail the run if they invent a year or a number.
highlights: Security-first ingest — posting text is attacker input on its way into a prompt, so raw bytes are vaulted (never rendered or sent to a model), HTML is sanitized, and every posting is screened for prompt injection, secret leaks and exfiltration, then allowed, redacted or blocked with the decision logged
Explainable deterministic scoring, not LLM scoring — a reproducible 0–100 fit over skills, keywords, seniority and location with a reason per factor; 👍/👎 rankings adjust scores by at most ±15

Grounded tailoring — resumes and cover letters are written from your own saved resume under a no-new-facts prompt, then checked: a year or number that is not in your material fails the run after one correction pass, and new names are listed for review
Git for your resume — every tailoring run produces a new version with a parent chain and a rendered diff
Application tracking — stages, notes, follow-up dates and an overdue banner, plus interview prep from your resume and documents
Runs on the lab's local models through the router under its own key; a deterministic mock model is the default for tests
1.9.0 security pass — loopback-only API (DNS-rebinding guard), CSRF refusal, strict CSP, upload size caps and generic error pages
stack: local models through the lab's LiteLLM router

projects.title: Crucible — WASM Training-Data Refinery
projects.summary: Security-first multimodal training-data refinery that treats every inbound byte as hostile: content is inspected exclusively inside import-free WebAssembly kernels (wasmtime), never on the host. Deterministic CLEAN/QUARANTINE/REJECT verdicts, a sha256-chained tamper-evident audit log, a sha-addressed content store, and a real cross-language kernel story — Rust compiled std-only to wasm32 under a blocked crates.io, hand-written WAT for simple kernels, and runtime parity gates across wasmtime and Node.
highlights: Hostile-content-first architecture: parsers are WASM kernels with zero imports (no fs/net/clock/WASI), so a kernel bug cannot exfiltrate or escape — OOB access traps inside wasmtime — and the host never interprets untrusted bytes (magic_fmt, zip_inspect, media_meta, entropy all run in-kernel)

Deterministic verdicts with fail-closed policy: same bytes always produce the same verdict, unknown rules fall closed to QUARANTINE, and every decision lands in a hash-chained audit log — hash = sha256(prev_hash + canonical(entry)), HMAC-SHA256 keyed when key material is present, with key rotation joining the chain and multi-key per-segment verification

Blocked-sandbox engineering workaround: crates.io and static.rust-lang.org were 403 from the sandbox, so the Rust tier was built on the host (Rust 1.99.0 + wasm32-unknown-unknown std target) with a strict std-only design — zero crates.io deps, in-repo std-only SHA-256, chain verifier, and canonical JSON (a custom panic handler conflicts with std's wasm build, error E0152)

Three kernel tiers by fit: Rust (one module, same ABI, 30,371-byte crucible_wasm.wasm, 18/18 host tests green incl. golden parity), hand-written WAT for simple kernels (crc32 and xorsum, 15/15 pytest plus 7/7 Node runtime-parity checks, WAT magic_fmt smoke 11/11), and Zig tier with a documented miscompile workaround (ziglang 0.17's std.mem.eql wasm32 backend miscompares runtime-derived slices — kernels use explicit byte-wise compares)

The whole refinery is operator-friendly and fail-closed end to end: crucible.cli ships store/clean/train/quarantine/audit-key/check commands, quarantined items require an explicit reviewer promote/deny appended to the same chain, dataset manifests bind training bytes to the audit log with sha-bound, path-contained, TOCTOU-guarded verification, and one-shot crucible check chains posture verdicts (exit 0 ok / 3 spike / 2 fail)

projects.title: Engine Console — one page for GPU inference engines
projects.summary: A control plane for vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp and Ollama across one or several machines. Each machine's own policy file decides whether the console may only watch it or also change it.
highlights: A hub talks to a small agent on every machine (ecnode) over a restricted ssh key; the node does all Docker, GPU and file work and obeys a local policy file, so a bug in the hub can do at most what each machine's policy allows

Five engines behind one adapter port, each with a pinned image — vLLM 0.27.1, SGLang 0.5.20, TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1, llama.cpp b10156 by digest, Ollama 0.30.11 — and launch forms generated from each adapter's parameter catalog
Engines run on an internal Docker network with no ports and all capabilities dropped, reachable only through a per-instance loopback gateway
A cross-machine model library: Hugging Face search and download, copies between machines, and a VRAM fit estimate that says "unknown" instead of guessing
Engines started by your own scripts are discovered read-only and shown beside managed ones, so the console never bypasses an existing start-up script
Learn mode: every setting carries a plain-language explanation, with a beginner wizard and a glossary
Honest status: the README lists what was verified live (one workstation, two GPUs) and what has only run against fakes (remote machines, launches of engines other than vLLM)
projects.html:
I run several inference engines on a workstation with two RTX PRO 6000s, next to a second GPU machine and four DGX Sparks. Every engine had its own start script, its own flags and its own way of reporting memory. Engine Console puts them on one page without taking over: it watches by default, and each machine decides for itself, in a root-owned policy file, whether the console may start, stop, download or delete anything there.

How it is built

  • Hub and node. The hub is a FastAPI app on loopback with a zero-build browser UI. It never runs Docker or reads /proc itself. Every machine, including its own, is reached through ecnode, a standard-library Python agent, over stdio locally and over ssh with a key restricted to that one command elsewhere.
  • Policy as the hard boundary. monitor or manage mode, allowed images, model roots and scripts are set per machine. The node re-reads its policy within seconds; the hub cannot edit it.
  • Engine isolation. Engines are labelled sibling containers on an --internal network with --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges and a pids limit. The hub reaches an engine's API only through its node.
  • Security posture. Loopback is not trusted (API key, Host, Origin and CSRF checks on every call), secrets are stored as [set] markers or 0600 files, and model files are confined to the policy's roots.

What is not done yet

The README is explicit: remote machines over ssh, copies between real machines, multi-GPU launches and launches of any engine but vLLM have run only against fakes. No penetration test or independent review has been done.

projects.title: System Monitor MCP Fleet
projects.summary: Three monitoring services, zero runtime dependencies — an MCP query server, an alerting server, and a dashboard, all built on Python's standard library.
highlights: 8 MCP tools for CPU, memory, disk, network, processes, uptime, health verdicts and a full snapshot — exact integer bytes from /proc and statvfs, CPU% from a two-sample /proc/stat delta

Every reading flows through a keyword-free module-level seam the tests monkeypatch with fixture files, so known-answer assertions (exact CPU%, exact memory bytes, exactly 2 violations on a breach fixture) pass identically under any machine load
Alert rules persist in a private sqlite db via ALERT_MCP_DB; the server refuses to open kanban.db/tasks.db and never writes outside /tmp, and the CLI exits 2 when any rule fires
The dashboard imports the two MCP modules read-only — neither file modified — and mounts HTML, /metrics, /tasks and /alerts routes; its tests use starlette TestClient with tmp dbs only
Hardened 2026-10-07 under mypy strict after an initial 2026-07-10 FastMCP build

projects.title: GPU Tuner — power caps, fan curves and clock caps with a GUI
projects.summary: A local web page that shows every NVIDIA GPU live and changes the three settings that are safe on any card. It manages several machines over ssh, and each machine's root daemon enforces its own limits.
highlights: Power limit, fan curve and core clock cap per card, plus a combined power budget per machine; going over the budget is a confirmed soft limit, never past the card's own hardware range

Every write is validated by a root daemon against a root-owned safety module, never by the page; the page runs as the desktop user and talks to the daemon over a Unix socket that checks the caller's uid
Fan safety floor rescaled per card from that card's own slowdown threshold (85 °C on the lab's RTX PRO 6000s); fans are handed back to the driver on exit, crash or watchdog kill
One page for several machines: a fleet strip plus a tab per machine, reached over ssh with the page's own key restricted to one command and one source address
Measured on four DGX Sparks: NVML exposes no power limit, fans or clock list there, so Sparks join as monitor-only nodes and the page says why
Deliberately not containerized: rootless Docker maps container root to the desktop user, verified to get "Insufficient Permissions" on power writes even with --privileged
projects.html:
Two RTX PRO 6000s in one workstation need power caps and a fan curve that survive reboots, driver resets and suspend. The lab first had two systemd services with numbers baked in. GPU Tuner replaces them with a page that shows what each card is doing and why its clock is limited, and lets you change only what is safe, with the root daemon as the single authority.

The safety model

  • Power: each card's own NVML range, narrowed by a measured profile where one exists, then the machine's combined budget. Lowering is always allowed.
  • Fans: any curve is evaluated as max(requested, floor(temperature)), with hysteresis (up at once, down only after 2 °C of cooling) and the floor re-asserted every 30 seconds.
  • Clocks: a cap can only slow the card down.
  • Left out on purpose: clock offsets, thermal targets and toggling ECC, MIG or compute mode — no range is known to be stable across arbitrary hardware.

The installer has a --dry-run that prints every privileged command, rolls back on any failure, and --uninstall restores the services it replaced.

projects.title: ds_core Data Science Toolkit
projects.summary: Pure-Python data science toolkit on the DuckDB CLI subprocess — 38 modules, no numpy, no duckdb binding. A five-reviewer audit confirmed 26 bugs (5 critical); every one fixed and verified.
highlights: 38 modules, all running on stdlib + subprocess calls to the duckdb binary — genuine Lloyd's k-means, power-iteration PCA, Lee & Seung NMF, logistic-loss gradient boosting, bootstrap random forests, all hand-rolled and audit-verified

2026-07-12 full-codebase audit by 5 reviewers found 26 confirmed findings (5 CRITICAL, 16 HIGH, 4 MEDIUM, 1 LOW); all fixed with 72 inline AUDIT FIX comments, plus 3 extra bugs surfaced only while verifying

Fixes proven by measurement, not inspection — t-SNE same-cluster 5-NN accuracy 0.57 to 0.97, UMAP cluster separation chance to 1.0, AutoML selection leakage removed (validation 0.95 vs honest test 0.90), new Platt/isotonic calibrators cut ECE 0.221 to 0.019
Security hardening in the same pass — HTML/JS escaping in report and dashboard generators, a trusted_sql opt-in gate on Pipeline.load, and path-traversal refusal in the model downloader
One honest gap: the seeded fractional-sample test intermittently fails its tolerance band — 294/295 tests pass on a fresh 2026-10-08 run and the flake is documented, not deleted

projects.title: Gov Payroll Analytics Workbench
projects.summary: Analytics pipeline over a 23-table, ~279M-row ClickHouse database of government payroll and federal spending: 14 re-runnable probe datasets that embed their own SQL, plus a self-contained dashboard.
highlights: The agent doing the analysis has no database port by design — the query layer drives the clickhouse-mcp server over JSON-RPC with SSE responses, session-id handshakes, retry and stale-session re-handshake
Every dataset is self-documenting — each data/*.json embeds the exact SQL, per-attempt elapsed time and row count, and the dashboard ships a provenance section exposing all of it

Three real ClickHouse quirks diagnosed and worked around — missing arbitrary() (error 46), alias-shadowing ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION (error 184), and non-uniform column names like fiscal_year stored as the string FY2026

Two coverage traps caught before they lied — QCEW carries 9 aggregation levels per county (~9x overstate unless filtered to agglvl_code 70) and federal awards store cumulative modifications (~12x overstate until deduped to final obligation per award)
KPIs are recomputed from the rows at build time, never hardcoded; the single index.html embeds data as a JSON island and opens over file:// with zero network requests

projects.title: Langfuse Observability Dashboard
projects.summary: Air-gapped dashboard for Langfuse traces: a re-runnable fetch pipeline, KPIs and a trace drill-down. Its broker blocks data reads (403), so it ships an honest empty state with the 403 recorded verbatim.
highlights: Idempotent fetch pipeline: atomic rewrites, page- and cursor-based pagination, ~5000-item caps per collection
Credentials from environment only; no secret ever printed or written to disk
Single-file dashboard, zero network requests, data embedded as a JS const so it opens over file://
Trace explorer drills into the observations parent/child tree with latency, usage and I/O previews
Verified broker behaviour endpoint by endpoint: health/projects OK, traces/observations/sessions/scores all 403 — failure recorded, nothing fabricated

projects.title: Model Quality Harness
projects.summary: Deterministic tool-calling reliability benchmark for local LLMs behind an OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM broker. Eight fixed scenarios, simulated tool execution, rule-by-rule scoring with no LLM judge — and a dashboard from real results.
highlights: 8-scenario fixed suite: single-tool lookups, multi-constraint calls, two-step dependencies, and a retry scenario where the simulator rejects the first call
Deterministic judge only — schema-valid tool-call JSON, parameter accuracy under normalization, and success criteria like call_made / params_exact / param_absent / answer_contains
Tracks silent failures HTTP 200 hides: empty_content_turns, reasoning_burn_turns (finish_reason=length with content null), finish_reason per turn
Proved the broker response-cached identical request bodies (~0.01 s replays); cache-busting user stamps restored real latency distributions (min 0.83 s / median 1.29 s / max 3.72 s)
Broker outages are recorded as failures with the real HTTP error body, never papered over

projects.title: Code Quality Metrics MCP
projects.summary: AST-based Python code-quality metrics over FastMCP — complexity, imports, bare excepts and parameter lists, stdlib-only. Its own scanner flagged its own code, and the findings were fixed.
highlights: Cyclomatic complexity straight from the AST — branch points counted for If, IfExp, For, While, ExceptHandler, With, Assert plus BoolOp AND/OR chains

Three anti-pattern detectors (bare except, print instead of logging, functions over 5 params) turned into file- and function-level alerts with warning/error severities at configurable thresholds (default complexity 10, LOC 500)
Four MCP tools — scan a directory, query files by complexity/LOC ranges, compare two directories, list threshold breaches; the recursive scanner skips venv, __pycache__ and node_modules
Dogfooding closed the loop — its own scan flagged print statements and bare excepts in this codebase, and a follow-up commit replaced them with logging on 2026-08-04
Complexity of the scanner itself was refactored down (72 to 66 total, alert logic 9 to 7) under test coverage

projects.title: DuckDB MCP Server
projects.summary: MCP server exposing 15 DuckDB tools — query, schema, import/export, profiling, cross-database — over stdio JSON-RPC. It drives the DuckDB CLI binary via subprocess and encodes 9 benchmark-proven best practices.
highlights: 15 tools spanning query, DDL/DML, CSV/Parquet import-export, profiling, ATTACH-based cross-DB joins
CLI subprocess over the Python binding: no version drift, -json output parsed with recursive type coercion to int/float/bool/None
Multi-statement SQL via temp files and duckdb -f, dodging argument-length limits
9 benchmark-proven best practices as code (bulk insert via generate_series: 100K users in 27 ms; 3x100K cross-DB join in 8 ms; Parquet at ~27% of CSV size), each pinned by an integration test
Pitfall guard for the real DuckDB failure mode: IDENTITY/SERIAL fails, so auto-increment goes through CREATE SEQUENCE + nextval()

projects.title: Multi-MCP Orchestrator
projects.summary: One CLI over six imported MCP servers — telemetry, tasks, wiki search, DuckDB analytics — as ten subcommands with chained pipelines and DuckDB trend queries. Plus a sandbox-wide wiki engine.
highlights: Direct Python import of six MCP server modules bypasses stdio/JSON-RPC overhead for same-process composition
Single _call_tool dispatcher normalizes divergent handler return shapes (tuple-with-dict vs list-of-TextContent) behind asyncio.run wrapping
Chained pipeline actions: scan, find, tasks, wiki, db, trends run as one command
Documented integration pitfalls: import order after sys.path setup, _tool_manager._tools vs _tool_map, dispatcher registration order

aiCapabilities.title: Local LLM inference on a six-machine GPU lab
aiCapabilities.summary: Open-weight models served on my own hardware: two RTX PRO 6000s, four DGX Sparks and an RTX 5090. Every model sits behind one router, and every engine is measured before it is trusted.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Qwen and Nemotron models on vLLM, SGLang and Dynamo across a heterogeneous GPU lab — with the operator tools I needed released as open source.
howItWorks: A workstation with two 96 GB RTX PRO 6000s runs the big local model across both cards (GLM-5.3-Flash with tensor parallelism over PCIe, about a 1M-token window), picked with one script that stops whatever else is loaded and starts engines in a safe order.

Four DGX Sparks join as one engine (tensor parallel across all four over ConnectX-7) for models too big for one box — DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in NVFP4 with speculative decoding, or the Nemotron models — with weights read from the workstation over NFS.
An RTX 5090 in a second machine serves the fast Nemotron Lightning model that answers first and judges routing.

Every engine sits behind the LiteLLM router as an alias, so switching models changes no client; Prometheus scrapes every engine and every machine's DCGM exporter, Grafana shows tokens, queues, KV cache and GPU temperature, and Nemo Console runs AIPerf load tests, NeMo Evaluator benchmarks and per-GPU DCGM diagnostics.
Kernels are checked per GPU architecture — the RTX PRO 6000s and the 5090 share sm_120, so one NVFP4 checkpoint and the same flags run on both, while the Sparks (sm_121) need their own builds.

proof.claim: Engine Console — open-source control plane for vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp and Ollama across machines
GPU Tuner — open-source power caps, fan curves and clock caps for the lab's GPUs, with per-card safety limits
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on four Sparks at about 67 tokens/s single-stream for code; moving its lookup tables to 16K records on NFS roughly halved prefill time (100K-token prompt 36 s to 20 s)
Model share over NFS to three Sparks from about 9 to 15.3 GB/s by finding ZFS cache churn on the server, not the NIC that was first blamed
Nemo Console 0.3.1 — DCGM telemetry for all six machines, per-GPU diagnostics, AIPerf load tests and NeMo Evaluator benchmarks from one page
A probe that sends a real completion before declaring an engine up — health endpoints stay 200 when one rank of a multi-node engine has died

limits: One big model at a time on the workstation; switching takes minutes of loading, and nothing schedules it automatically.
The Sparks run one lane at a time (GLM, Nemotron or DeepSeek), and the hottest node needs long benchmarks paused at 82 °C GPU or 90 °C SoC.
Single-tenant — it serves my agents and apps, not a team, and there is no autoscaling or high availability.
There is no cloud fallback — when every engine a route can use is down, the route fails.
aiCapabilities.html:
Serving open-weight models is the easy part. Knowing what is actually up, how fast, and why something failed is the work, and most of it is measurement: counting bytes at the NIC instead of trusting client-reported rates, profiling the NFS server under real multi-client load before blaming hardware, and sending a real completion instead of trusting a health check.

The machines

MachineGPUsRole
Workstation (Threadripper PRO, 246 GB RAM)2× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 96 GB eachthe main local model (tensor parallel across both), the router, observability, model storage over NFS
Four DGX SparksGB10, 128 GB unified memory eachone tensor-parallel engine across all four for the largest models
Second workstationRTX 5090, 32 GBthe fast routing tier and judge; video rendering when idle

The machines share a ConnectX-7 fabric. The workstation's two cards have no NVLink, so tensor parallelism between them runs over PCIe peer-to-peer, which needs iommu=pt on the kernel command line — a check script proves it after every kernel or BIOS change.

aiCapabilities.title: Smart routing — a fast model first, a judge, every call traced
aiCapabilities.summary: Every agent and app in my lab reaches models through one router. A fast model answers first, and an LLM judge sends the hard conversations to a bigger one.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: One router for every client, tier routing with an LLM judge (NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard), and a gateway that counts and traces each routed call — tuned by reading the answers, not the counters.
howItWorks: Every client — coding agents, the chat UI, the eval harness, the job-search app — calls only a LiteLLM router. It holds each client's own key, masks personal data in model output, and traces every call. Models are aliases, so no client knows which GPU serves it.

Tier routes put a fast model in front. Nemotron Lightning on an RTX 5090 answers first; GLM-5.3-Flash on two RTX PRO 6000s takes the conversations the judge scores as too hard. A second route escalates to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on four DGX Sparks.

The judge (Switchyard's classifier in capability mode) estimates the chance that the fast model can finish the task. Below 0.7 the conversation goes to the big model, and a verdict that fails to parse also goes to the big model.
It judges once per conversation, keyed on the first user message, so follow-up turns skip the judge — about ten times faster on repeated turns.
Coding agents name route ids on the NeMo Relay gateway instead of plain model names, so every routed call is counted and traced. Nemo Console and the Grafana boards show which tier served what.

proof.claim: Nemo Console, the open-source console that monitors Switchyard and Relay and edits their routes with validation and automatic rollback (0.3.0 manages ten NVIDIA systems)
Five routing configurations benchmarked on the same 12 tasks; the live one keeps tasks the fast model answers correctly on the 5090 and sends the uncertain ones to GLM

Found why the fast tier answered empty — the Anthropic-format path dropped the "thinking off" flag — and moved it to the OpenAI format; its hard-task answers became complete and 2.5–4× faster than the big model's
Session affinity measured on the live route — repeat turns reused the first decision with zero judge calls (p50 82–3,887 ms down to 17–157 ms)
Per-client router keys, so spend and traffic are attributed to each agent in Grafana and Langfuse

limits: The judge's packaged rubric does not describe this stack well — it sends some trivial one-liners ("What is 42?") to the big model. A custom rubric moves the profile, but crudely.
The judge is not fully deterministic; borderline verdicts flip between runs, so a difference of under about two tasks in twelve is noise.
Affinity keys on the first user message, so two conversations with the same opening share one routing decision.
On Switchyard 0.3.0 a judged route fails while its judge is down; it does not fall back to a single model.
Answers were checked by reading them, not by a graded quality score — 12 tasks are a sanity check, not an eval.
aiCapabilities.html:
Three layers, three jobs

LayerJob
LiteLLM router (:4000)The one door. Per-client keys and spend, a PII guardrail on output, OpenTelemetry traces to Langfuse and Tempo. Every model is an alias here.
Switchyard server (:4010)NVIDIA's routing server as a container: tier routes for clients that only speak to the router.
NeMo Relay gateway (:4040)A host service whose built-in Switchyard plugin routes the coding agents. Naming a route id instead of a plain model is what makes it count and trace the call.

What I learned getting it right

  • Benchmark answers, not tier counters. The counters said the fast tier was serving its share. The captured answers were empty: all 500 tokens went to hidden reasoning.
  • The wire format is behavior. The same model with the same flags thought instead of answering when the request went through the Anthropic-format translation, because that path dropped the flag that turns thinking off.
  • The rubric is the product. Swapping the judge for a much larger model kept the same backwards profile, and changing a two-sentence rubric moved it. The judge model is a commodity; the rubric is where the policy lives.
  • Judge once per conversation. Judging every request of an agent loop re-judges the same task twenty times.

The full account, with the benchmark tables, is in the write-up below.

aiCapabilities.title: The stack underneath the work
aiCapabilities.summary: Every capability on this site runs on one lab: six GPU machines on a ConnectX-7 fabric, one model router, and observability and containment around every agent. This page is the inventory and the reasons.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: The hardware and software behind every capability here — GPUs, engines, the routing layer, tracing and the sandboxes the agents run in — with the reasoning for each choice.
howItWorks: One door for models. Every client calls a LiteLLM router; it holds the per-client keys, the output PII guardrail and the tracing, so moving a model between machines changes no client.
A routing layer in front of the models. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard decides which tier serves a conversation, and the NeMo Relay gateway counts and traces each routed call from the coding agents.
Engines chosen per model and card. vLLM, SGLang and Dynamo on the workstation and the Sparks, llama.cpp and Ollama for experiments — pinned images, rootless Docker, engines on internal networks.
Observability before anything else. OpenTelemetry traces go to Tempo, Langfuse and Phoenix; Prometheus and Loki feed Grafana; alerts land in a private chat room.

Containment by default. Egress is denied unless a host is on an allowlist, each MCP server runs in its own sandbox, untrusted scripts run in NVIDIA OpenShell sandboxes, a NeMo Guardrails server checks prompts and answers, agents get scoped keys from brokers instead of real ones, and secrets are encrypted before they touch disk.

proof.claim: Engine Console — the open-source control plane for the engines
GPU Tuner — the open-source power, fan and clock tool for the GPUs
Nemo Console 0.3.1 — the open-source console for ten of these NVIDIA systems (Switchyard, Relay, Dynamo, DCGM, AIPerf, NeMo Guardrails, OpenShell, SkillEvaluator, NeMo Evaluator, Data Designer)
Agent Hub — the open-source control plane for what each agent knows and may do
This site — React 19, Vite and TypeScript, prerendered to static HTML and deployed by GitHub Actions

limits: Single operator, single tenant — built for my agents and apps, not a team.
Model placement is manual — one big model on the workstation at a time and one lane on the Sparks at a time.
Rootless Docker cannot reach host-published ports from a container, so services talk over a shared Docker network, and tools that need real root (GPU power limits) run on the host.
No autoscaling or high availability anywhere.
Host-level security templates (auditd, AppArmor, nftables) are opt-in and applied by hand, never automatically.

aiCapabilities.html:
Every capability page on this site describes work done on one physical lab. This page is the inventory underneath all of them.

Agents that use the lab

Claude Code (also in a bubblewrap-sandboxed variant that runs on local models), opencode, Codex, Hermes Agent, Turnstone and Open WebUI all reach the models through the router with their own keys. Agent Hub keeps their skills, instructions and permissions in one reviewed git repository, and lab-chat — a private Matrix server — is how they notify me, ask for approval and hand work to each other.

aiCapabilities.title: Video generation with LTX-2.5 on local GPUs
aiCapabilities.summary: Short films with synchronized speech, rendered by LTX-2.5 on three local GPUs and driven by an agent. Faces come from a reference image and voices from reference audio, and every clip is checked before it ships.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: LTX-2.5 (22B, NVFP4) on ComfyUI across two RTX PRO 6000s and an RTX 5090 — native speech and lip sync, a multi-shot film pipeline, and per-clip checks for speech, voice and silence.
howItWorks: Three ComfyUI render workers — one per RTX PRO 6000 on the main workstation and one on the RTX 5090 in a second machine — load the same NVFP4 weights from one NFS share; all three cards are sm_120, so the same image and kernels run everywhere.

A shot list becomes one generation per shot, pulled off a shared queue so the faster card takes more shots; two to four connected shots can be rendered in a single generation when one character must hold across cuts.
LTX-2.5 generates speech and lip sync natively from the prompt. The face is anchored by a reference image and the voice by a reference audio clip — the two are independent and compose.
Prompts are written as prose, the way the model's guide asks — shot, scene, action, character, camera and audio in one paragraph, spoken lines in quotes, a beat of stillness before speech.
Every clip is verified, not sampled — transcribed with Whisper to catch wrong or repeated lines, compared against the reference voice, and checked for unwanted speech in cutaways.
An agent drives it — the video skills run in Turnstone (moved from a Hermes Agent setup), reaching ComfyUI and the GPUs only through brokers, and finished films are exported from its sandbox.

proof.claim: A text-to-video render on the RTX 5090 completes in 70–80 s, including the first load of the 18.7 GB transformer over NFS
Across five film builds, 22 of 24 shots passed their checks on the first try; the two failures were prompt-bound and passed after rewording
Native multi-shot generation held the voice within a 12.1 Hz pitch spread, against 41–68 Hz for every stitching scheme tried
Cutaways with no people in frame stayed silent in 18 of 19 renders; a person on screen talks even when told not to

limits: The renders stay in the lab; there are no public samples yet.
Voice consistency is measured with a pitch proxy, not a speaker-embedding model, and its threshold has not been calibrated against listening tests.
The GPUs are shared with the language models — the 5090 runs either the routing tier or ComfyUI, and the workstation cards render only when the big model leaves room.
On the 5090 (32 GB) the model, text encoder and VAEs do not fit at once; the text encoder is evicted to host RAM between steps.
Chained continuations decay past about eight clips and can repeat a quoted line, so long scenes are cut into one generation per shot.
aiCapabilities.html:
The first conclusion here was wrong, and it is worth recording: I decided the model could not do dialogue without a separate text-to-speech stage, from reading node descriptions. One render with a quoted line in the prompt showed synchronized speech. Test the capability before declaring it missing.

Measurement mistakes that cost four rebuilds

  • A visual fix judged with an audio metric. Seeding each shot from a reference image was scored on voice pitch, called worse, and dropped. It was the right fix for the face all along. Match the measure to the mechanism.
  • Sampling hid half a defect. Checking only the first clip of each speaking shot showed five clean matches while half the dialogue clips were broken.
  • The metric became the target. Making "no speech" the pass condition for cutaways produced dead air. Asking for specific background sound fixed it.

Watching the output caught what four rounds of instrumentation missed.

aiCapabilities.title: Data analytics on a 279M-row ClickHouse database
aiCapabilities.summary: Fourteen re-runnable probe datasets over Massachusetts payroll, PPP loans, federal spending, employment, property and income data in ClickHouse. Each embeds its own SQL and timings, and two traps that inflate totals 9–12× were caught before they reached a chart.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: 23 tables and ~279M rows in ClickHouse, reached by an agent only through an MCP server; 14 self-documenting datasets, every query under 0.3 s, and one dashboard file that needs no network.
howItWorks: Map each table's grain and coverage before querying — state payroll, municipal payroll, BLS QCEW employment, SBA PPP loans, federal awards, property parcels and IRS income by ZIP code.
Write self-documenting probe datasets — each output file embeds the exact SQL, the elapsed time of every attempt and the row count, so any number can be re-run and audited.

Reach the database only through an MCP server, by design — the agent doing the analysis has no database port, so the query layer handles the session handshake, retries and a fresh session when one goes stale.

Diagnose ClickHouse quirks instead of guessing — a missing arbitrary() aggregate (error 46), alias shadowing that raises ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION (error 184), and fiscal years stored as the string "FY2026".
Check totals against known figures before charting — QCEW and federal awards both overstated by an order of magnitude until filtered and deduplicated.

proof.claim: 14 probe datasets, each with its SQL, per-attempt timing and row count embedded
A single self-contained dashboard — a 51-tile US map, dual-axis trends and a provenance section listing every query
A query client for the MCP server with session handshake, retry and re-handshake
Two coverage traps documented with their fixes (QCEW aggregation levels and federal award modifications)

limits: The agent never touches the database directly; every query goes through the MCP server, which adds a hop.
Coverage is uneven — QCEW covers 2021–2024, state payroll 2009–2026, municipal payroll FY2011–FY2027 for at most four cities.
About 216M of the 279M rows are FEC campaign-finance tables that this work deliberately left out.
The dashboard is a snapshot (data embedded in one HTML file), not a live connection.
aiCapabilities.html:
A 23-table ClickHouse database covering Massachusetts government payroll, SBA PPP loans, federal spending, QCEW employment, property values and IRS income data. The interesting problems are not the queries — they are the coverage traps, the alias-shadowing errors and the grain mismatches that make naive analysis lie.

What the data covers

DomainTableCoverageScale
MA state payrollma_state_payroll2009–2026~137K employees a year
MA municipal payrollmunicipal_payrollFY2011–FY2027at most 4 cities
BLS QCEW employmentbls_qcew_ma2021–202414 counties
SBA PPP loanssba_ppp_loans2020–202111.5M loans, $797B
Federal awardsusaspendingFY2025–FY2026deduplicated to the final obligation
Property parcelsma_property_parcels—2.56M rows
IRS incomeirs_soi_zip2018–2022by ZIP code

Findings

Each figure comes from one probe dataset with its SQL embedded.

  • State payroll, 2026: 136,415 employees in 158 departments, $5.59B in wages. The 2009 data has a single department, so coverage varies a lot across the series. Largest employers: the University of Massachusetts system (23,399 employees, $918M) and the MBTA (8,796 employees, $506M).
  • PPP loans: 11.5M loans totalling $797B across 60 states and territories. California leads with 1.27M loans ($104B), Texas follows with 939K ($63B).
  • Property: the 100 highest-value towns hold 1.59M parcels worth $1.57T. Boston has 180K parcels ($265B); Cambridge has 29K ($93B), so its value per parcel ($3.2M) is more than double Boston's ($1.5M).
  • Employment (QCEW, Q4 of the latest year): Middlesex County employs 930K people with $26.3B in quarterly wages; Suffolk follows with 717K and $24.2B.

The two traps

  1. QCEW aggregation levels. The raw table carries nine aggregation levels per county. Without filtering to agglvl_code = 70 (county totals), employment comes out about nine times too high. It showed up because the numbers did not match known county populations.
  2. Federal award modifications. usaspending adds a row for every amendment with the full obligated amount, not the change. Without keeping only the final obligation per award, spending comes out about twelve times too high. It showed up when cross-checked against published totals.

The pipeline

The query layer drives a clickhouse-mcp server over JSON-RPC with server-sent-event responses. The dashboard is one HTML file with the data embedded — a 51-tile US map, dual-axis trends and a provenance section that lists every query, its elapsed time and its row count. It makes no network requests.
